Mahmudul Islam, Attorney General Bazlur Rahman Chhana, Aspirant Attorney-General with him) instructed by A. M. M. Sahidul Huq, Advocate-on-Record ----- For the Appellant 
Sharifuddin Chaklader, Advocate-on-Record ----- For the Appellant
parties:
The Registrar of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh Supreme Court Building Dhaka ----- Appellant
Vs.
Md. Shafiuddin, son of late Md. Asuruddin and another ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
2. Against the order of his removal from service the respondent filed case in the Administrative Tribunal who held that the charge was framed by an incompetent authority i.e. the Deputy Registrar-in-charge while the law empowers only the Registrar or any officer designated by the Chief Justice to frame the charge, but dismissed the case on a technical ground that the case was barred because no departmental appeal was filed. The Administrative Appellate Tribunal on the contrary held that in fact departmental appeal having been filed the case was not barred. The Administrative Appellate Tribunal further held that the enquiry was held in violation of the rules depriving the respondent of reasonable opportunity of self defence, that the enquiry was perfunctory resulting gross failure of justice and that the decision proposing punishment of removal from service against the respondent and his co-accused was arrived at by the Chief Justice, but the Chief Justice was not given to consider the reply of the respondent while the Registrar passed the order imposing a major penalty against the respondent, but acquitting the other imposing a minor penalty of censure. In view of the aforesaid findings the Administrative Appellate Tribunal allowed the appeal and declared the order of removal from service as illegal and void. 

 To consider this ground we are required to look into the Supreme Court of Bangladesh (High Court Division) Employees (Discipline and Appeal) Rules, 1983. These rules authorize the "Authority" to take action against an employee and rule 2(I) defines the "Authority" as "the Registrar or any officer of the court designated by the Chief Justice". It is the admitted position in the instant case that the charge was framed by he Deputy Registrar-in-charge and he was not designated by the Chief Justice for that purpose. Learned Attorney General argues that there cannot be any distinction between the Registrar and the Deputy Registrar-in-charge. I understand from this argument that the learned Attorney General is speaking about the apparent authority. It means that a legal power is vested in the person holding the charge of another in the absence of any legal intention that it should not exist. Therefore the power existed to the Deputy Registrar-in-charge for the routine works, but not for the particular purpose of framing the charge against an employee because rule 2(I) gives the Registrar such power as persona designate which means a person considered as an individual in algal action. Had it not bee so, there was no necessity of adding the words "or any officer of the Court designated by the Chief Justice" in the definition rule because in any event there shall be an officer in charge of the Registrar. Thus I find no substance in this ground. 

 6. Now let us see what is meant by misconduct in the Rules of 1983. Rule 2(2) defines misconduct as "the conduct prejudicial to good order or service discipline or unbecoming of an officer and gentleman". We must keep in mind that the respondent was not attached to the copying section and obviously he was not approached as being an employee in the copying section nor he pretended so which is clear from the complaint petition. He was approached as suggested by the clerk of the complainant's advocate. The charge against him that he demanded TK. 2,000/= for obtaining the certified copy. The complainant agreed to pay, but obviously did not pay and complained to the Chief Justice. 

 7. Mere demand of a big amount by a insignificant employee even not connected with the section concerned and introduced by the clerk of his advocate cannot infuriate a litigant to complain to the Chief Justice. The complainant did not tell the truth though being a retired general manager of Shilpa Bank he had much superior status in the society than the respondent. 

 It is the admitted position that instead of the Registrar, the Chief Justice himself proposed major punishment to both the accused, and accordingly second show cause notices were issued, but the Chief Justice was not given to consider the replies and the Registrar imposed the major punishment on the respondent and in fact acquitted the other. This action must be held to be malafide, biased and illegal. Thus this ground has got no merit. 

 11. Respondent No. 1 (herein after referred to as the Respondent) joined in the service as 'farash' in the then High Court of East Pakistan on December 10, 1968 and was provisionally promoted as peon on March 1,1972 and was confirmed in the said post on March 1,1974 and thereafter was promoted as record arranger on September 27, 1986 and that while discharging duty as the record arranger in the appeal section of the High Court Division a proceeding for the offence of misconduct under Rule 3(b) of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh (High Court Division) employees (Discipline and Appeal) Rules 1983, (hereinafter in short, the rules) was initiated on November, 1,1990 on the allegation that he demanded on October 31, 1990 a sum of TK. 2000/= as bribe from Mr. Naziruddin, respondent in First Appeal No. 32 of 1983, for supplying certified copy of the judgment of the said appeal. On November 15, 1990 the Respondent submitted a written statement of his defence denying the allegation. A Deputy Registrar of the High Court Division was appointed Enquiry Officer and upon holding enquiry he submitted his report on November 24, 1990 finding the Respondent guilty by the same report. The inquiry officer also found the Superintendent of the appeal section guilty since he supported the Respondent when Naziruddin Complained to him. Thereafter the Respondent was served with the 2nd notice dated October 27, 1990 by he Order of the Chief Justice and to that the Respondent replied pleading innocent. Ultimately the appellate passed the order dated January 26/27, 1991 removing the Respondent from service with effect from January 20, 1991. The Respondent as per provision of the Rules preferred appeal on February 4, 1991 to the Chief Justice of Supreme Court of Bangladesh and the said appeal was without any success the Respondent was informed of the disposal of the appeal by the letter dated May 14, 1991. 

 12. The Respondent to seek redress against the order of his removal from service filed Administrative Tribunal Case No. 155 of 1991 before the Administrative Tribunal, (AT), Dhaka, The same having been dismissed he preferred Appeal No. 63 of 1992 before the Administrative Appellate Tribunal, (AAT) Dhaka and the AAT upon allowing the appeal sent back the Administrative Tribunal Case, No. 155 of 1991 to the AT for disposal in accordance with law. The AT thereafter by its judgment and order dated July 23, 1996 dismissed the appeal on the findings that the Respondent did not prefer any appeal before the appellate authority and that no decision was taken by the appropriate appellate authority in the matter of imposition of penalty and thus the case was barred under the proviso to Section 4(2) of the Administrative Tribunal Act, 1980, (Act VII of 1981) (herein after in short the Act). As against the said judgment and order of the AT the Respondent filed Appeal No. 75 of 1996 before the AAT and the AAT by its judgment and order dated December, 9, 1998 allowed the appeal on the findings that the AT was in error in holding that the case of the Respondent (appellant before AAT) was barred under first proviso to Section 4(2) of the Act and that the entire proceeding was vitiated since the charge as against the respondent was framed by incompetent authority, i.e. Deputy Registrar, in charge of the office of the Registrar, and that the appellant (Respondent before A.A.T) could not show that the Deputy Registrar, in charge of the office of the Registrar was designated by the Chief Justice for the purpose of framing charge against the Respondent, that procedure adopted by the Enquiry Officer in holding the inquiry was somewhat peculiar in that the witnesses examined were cross-examined by the Enquiry Officer instead of by the Respondent, that Enquiry was held in violation of the Rules depriving the Respondent of reasonable opportunity of self defence and that enquiry being perfunctory resulted in failure of justice and as such order of removal "based on such perverse report cannot be sustainable in law", that although the Chief Justice passed the order for issuing the second show cause notice but the reply to the show cause notice was not placed before the Chief Justice and that the final order was passed by the Registrar, that "the consideration of the 2nd show cause reply by an authority subordinate to the authority issuing the notice proposing penalty tantamount to no consideration of the reply, which in turn results in deprivation of opportunity to show cause. If the other accused could be let of with the minimum punishment of censure by the subordinate authority, the scope for taking such lenient view on the part of the higher authority in the case of the applicant could not be ruled out." and that the Respondent was seriously prejudiced by the final order passed by the Respondent and consequent thereupon declared the order removing the Respondent from service illegal, void, inoperative and not binding upon him "and that he is still in service". 

 15. Mr. Sharifuddin Chaklader learned Advocate-on-Record appearing for the Respondent No. 1 has submitted that AAT was quite correct in holding that charge was framed against the Respondent by incompetent person i.e. neither by the Registrar nor by the officer of the Court designated by the Chief Justice and such entire proceeding against the Respondent was vitiated from its initial stage of initiation. He has also submitted that the inquiry that was conducted by the inquiry officer was somewhat queer in that the inquiry officer questioned the delinquent employee i.e. the Respondent and thereupon whatever statement was made that was recorded but without affording opportunity to cross-examine the witnesses examined by the authority nor allowed the Respondent to put on record evidence from his side and thus the Respondent having been denied of the guaranteed right of putting his defence either by cross-examining the witnesses examined by the authority or by examining witnesses of his choice as there was violation of principle of natural justice and the Rules and as such the punishment that was awarded by the Registrar without placing 2nd show cause notice before the Chief Justice as the same was issued at the direction of the Chief Justice, was illegal. 

 18. It is also not disputed the Deputy Registrar at the material time i.e. when the charge was framed against the Respondent, as 'in-charge,' being duly authorized by the competent authority, was performing the functions and discharging duties of the office of the Registrar and that being so in the light of the accepted rules of business of the office of a particular officer, in the instant case of the office of the Register of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh, the act of framing of charge against the Respondent was undoubtedly the action of the officer i.e. the Registrar of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh whose office Registrar 'in-charge' was holding and was performing the functions and discharging the duties thereof. It is also not seen from the record nor any material has been placed on record by the Respondent to show that he actions taken, functions performed and the duties discharged by the Registrar, in charge i.e. the Deputy Registrar, was not approved or accepted in any respect either by the Registrar on his assumption of office or by the authority, superior/higher, to the Registrar. That being the position in my view the AAT was in serious error in holding that the action of the Register, 'in-charge' framing charge of misconduct against the Respondent was an action of an incompetent authority or person. When an officer acts as 'in-charge' on being duly authorized by the competent authority/person, of an officer he in all intent and purport or in other words in all respects acts as an officer assigned to that office or post and performs the functions and duties of that offices an officer duly authorized and that unless specified that the 'in-charge' would perform only the assigned functions and duties but not the entire functions and duties of that office, which is not in the instant case, then whatever, action taken, functions performed or duties discharged would certainly be the action of the officer holding the office even though the officer is an 'in-charge. In the instant case nothing has been placed to show the Registrar in-charge, was authorized by the competent authority to perform only the designated functions and duties, rather it is seen that the Registrar, in charge, was authorized to perform the entire, functions and duties of the Registrar. That being the position it cannot be said as because charge was framed against the Respondent by the Registrar, in charge, and not by the Registrar or by an officer of the Court designated by the Chief justice as per sub-rule (1) of Rule 2 of the Rules, the proceeding from its very inception was aviated and consequent thereupon the enquiry that was directed, and the report that was submitted and that in the light of the inquiry report 2nd show cause notice that was served and finally decision for removing the respondent from the service taken were unsustainable in law. 

 21. The AAT was not founded in while setting aside the order of removal of the Respondent upon the view that the same was passed in violation of the principle of natural justice and the Rules in that proceeding against the Respondent was drawn by the Registrar in-charge, who in the light of the accepted Rule as well as practice was at the relevant time no less an officer than the Register and his action was no less than that of the Registrar and that as the Respondent replied to the charges framed against him without raising any objection of irregularity (supposed) and that the he was present during enquiry and replied to the 2nd show cause notice where in he admitted certain fact constituting misconduct and that the fact so admitted having had nexus to the substantive allegation constituting misconduct and that thereupon the competent authority passed order of removal. The AAT, as it appears from the judgment under appeal, was of the view as to violation of natural justice and the Rules because the Enquiry Officer recorded the statement of the Respondent by putting question to him and that some of the witnesses examined by the authority were not allowed to cross-examine by the respondent. Upon total consideration of the materials on record it is seen that even if the view that was taken by the AAT in the light of the matters as stated herein above is accepted then also it cannot be said that respondent was prejudiced in any respect since the material witnesses were examined in presence of the Respondent and he cross-examined them and that nothing was pointed from the evidence of the witnesses who said to have not been allowed to cross-examine either for obtaining fact in denial of the facts stated in chief or to elicit further facts relating to the facts stated by the witnesses in examination in chief to discredit them or to establish otherwise. It appears that the AAT was of the view that in proceeding against the Respondent there was violation of the Rules since the 2nd show cause notice was issued on the direction of the Chief Justice and in taking final decision for awarding punishment the same was not placed before the Chief Justice, but was considered by the Registrar (appellant) and finally he awarded the punishment. The fact being that it is the Registrar who is the competent authority in respect of the Respondent for taking disciplinary action and that the Registrar on consideration of the materials on record having made the decision for awarding punishment to the Respondent and having passed the order of removal the same in may view cannot be said to have been passed in violation of the Rules.
